nameStory: Marsh speedwell gets its name from its preferred wetland habitat and the old belief that speedwells could provide swift healing or 'speed you well' on your journey to recovery. The genus name Veronica comes from Saint Veronica, who according to legend wiped Christ's face with a cloth, connecting these delicate flowers to acts of mercy and healing.
description: Marsh speedwell is a delicate, low-growing perennial wildflower that thrives in New England's wet places. It produces small, pale blue to white flowers with four petals and reaches about 6-20 inches tall. The plant has a sprawling, somewhat trailing growth habit with narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in pairs along slender stems. You'll often find it forming loose mats in marshy areas and along pond edges.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny four-petaled flowers, usually pale blue or white with darker blue veins, about 1/4 inch across. They're arranged loosely along thin, wispy stalks that emerge from where leaves meet the stem.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Narrow, lance-shaped leaves arranged in opposite pairs along the stem. They feel smooth and slightly succulent, with a fresh, mild scent when crushed.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, mat-forming plant that often trails along wet ground or through shallow water. Stems feel soft and somewhat fleshy to the touch.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, flattened, heart-shaped seed capsules that split open when ripe, releasing tiny brown seeds.

habitat: Look for marsh speedwell in wet, marshy areas throughout New England - along pond edges, in boggy meadows, wet ditches, and shallow swampy spots. It prefers muddy or sandy soils that stay consistently moist and can tolerate having its roots in shallow standing water. You'll often find it growing alongside other wetland plants like sedges and rushes.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as temperatures warm, with fresh green leaves appearing in opposite pairs along developing stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, when the delicate pale blue flowers are most visible and diagnostic.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and seed capsules mature, splitting open to release seeds. Foliage may begin to yellow.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to underground portions in cold climates, leaving little trace above ground until spring returns.

funFact: Marsh speedwell can actually root from its leaf nodes when stems touch wet soil, essentially cloning itself as it sprawls across marshy ground - making it a natural wetland engineer that helps stabilize muddy shorelines!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with American brooklime, another wetland speedwell, but marsh speedwell has much narrower leaves and paler, more delicate flowers. Remember: marsh speedwell has skinny leaves like marsh grass, while brooklime has broader, more oval leaves.
contextualKnowledge: The speedwell family has a confusing history - it was recently moved from the Figwort family (Scrophulariaceae) to the Plantain family (Plantaginaceae) based on DNA studies, so you might see it listed under either family in older field guides.
compareHints: Among the speedwells, marsh speedwell is distinctive for its wetland habitat and very narrow leaves. Most other speedwells like thyme-leaved speedwell prefer drier soils and have rounder leaves, while American brooklime shares the wet habitat but has much broader, oval leaves. The pale, washed-out flower color also sets marsh speedwell apart from the brighter blues of many of its relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's speedwells, heath speedwell is unique for its distinctly creeping, mat-forming growth habit and very fuzzy stems and leaves.
Among New England's speedwells, thyme-leaved speedwell is unique in its strongly creeping, mat-forming habit - most other speedwells grow more upright.
Among the speedwells, germander speedwell stands out for having the brightest blue flowers and the most prominent flower stalks that clearly rise above the foliage.
Among the speedwells, corn speedwell is distinguished by its fuzzy leaves and very small size - it's one of the tiniest in the genus.
Bird's-eye speedwell stands out from its many speedwell relatives by having the brightest, most intensely blue flowers with the most prominent dark radiating lines.
Among the many speedwells in New England, American brooklime is the water-lover of the group.
Among New England's many speedwell species, purslane speedwell stands out for its highly variable leaf shapes on a single plant and its preference for the most disturbed habitats.
Unlike the upright thyme-leaved speedwell or the larger-flowered Germander speedwell, slender speedwell stays flat to the ground with its characteristic thread-thin stems.

Long-leaved Speedwell towers over most other New England speedwells - while species like Thyme-leaved Speedwell hug the ground and Germander Speedwell stays low in lawns, this species stands tall with substantial flower spikes.
Unlike most other New England speedwells that are annual weeds or die back completely in winter, creeping speedwell is a true perennial that forms permanent mats.

Among New England speedwells, broadleaf speedwell stands out for its relatively large, oval leaves and dense flower spikes - most other speedwells have much smaller, narrower leaves and more open flower arrangements.
Among New England's many speedwells, blue water-speedwell is unique in its aquatic lifestyle - while American brooklime also likes wet areas, it grows taller and has larger flowers.
Among New England's speedwells, ivy-leaved speedwell is easily distinguished by its distinctive lobed leaves that look like tiny ivy leaves.
Unlike its lowland speedwell relatives that grow in fields and gardens, American alpine speedwell is the mountain specialist of the family.
Spiked speedwell towers over its New England speedwell relatives, most of which are small, creeping, or prostrate plants with much smaller flower clusters.
Among the many speedwells in New England, Pink Ivy-leaved Speedwell stands out for its distinctly lobed, ivy-like leaves - most other speedwells have simple, unlobed leaves.
Grey field-speedwell stands out from its speedwell relatives primarily by its grayish leaf color and extremely small size.
Among the speedwells, chain speedwell is unique for its strong preference for aquatic habitats and its creeping, often floating growth habit.
